title: How Extinction Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain extinction as a natural process: early beliefs that God's creation could not go extinct, George Cuvier's 1812 catastrophism, Darwin's gradual-extinction view, and Walter and Luis Alvarez's asteroid hypothesis for the dinosaurs. They cover background extinction rates, fossil record gaps, Lazarus species (coelacanth, Cuban solenodon, Gilbert's potoroo, Bermuda petrel), pseudo-extinction, causes of extinction (habitat loss, competition, hunting, contaminants), the passenger pigeon and Buffalo, de-extinction (Bucardo, woolly mammoth), the Big Five mass extinctions, and the debate over the ongoing sixth mass extinction (human-caused overkill versus climate change), including ocean acidification and jellyfish booms. The episode ends with listener mail about police interrogation and a mock trial.

entities.name: Revolutions on the Surface of the Globe

segments.title: Opening banter and reading list
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the episode topic and mention Busta Rhymes, then recommend reading: Elizabeth Kolbert's New Yorker piece and book The Sixth Extinction, a New York Review of Books piece on jellyfish, and earlier HowStuffWorks articles.

segments.title: Beliefs about extinction and Cuvier
segments.summary: Religious views that God's creation could not go extinct, Thomas Jefferson's search for mastodons, George Cuvier's 1812 essay on lost species and catastrophic events, and Darwin's view of slow, gradual extinction.

segments.title: Alvarez asteroid hypothesis and the dinosaurs
segments.summary: Walter Alvarez studied the iridium-rich clay layer at the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary, proposed an asteroid impact in 1980, faced resistance, and was supported when the Yucatan crater was dated. The event is now called the Cretaceous-Paleogene event, ending the Mesozoic and starting the Cenozoic.

segments.title: Natural extinction rates and the fossil record
segments.summary: Species typically last about ten million years. Background extinction rates are estimated at a low level per million species per year, now thought to be a hundred to a thousand times higher. Gaps in the fossil record make counts uncertain, and scientists use math models and the idea of minimum viable population.

segments.title: Lazarus species and pseudo-extinction
segments.summary: Coelacanth rediscovery off South Africa and Madagascar is discussed as a Lazarus species. Pseudo-extinction, where a species evolves into a new one, is considered. Other rediscovered species are mentioned, and the hosts note that uncertainty about living species counts remains.

segments.title: Causes of extinction and the passenger pigeon
segments.summary: Habitat change, competition, hunting, and contaminants are the main causes, and humans contribute to all four. Extinction can cascade through ecosystems, illustrated by the stellar sea cow and the passenger pigeon, whose population boomed after its native predators died from disease and was then hunted to extinction.

segments.title: De-extinction and the Bucardo
segments.summary: The 2003 cloning of the Bucardo, a Spanish mountain goat, survived only minutes. The hosts discuss the moral question of bringing back extinct animals such as the woolly mammoth and the risk of reducing efforts to protect species now.

segments.title: The Big Five mass extinctions
segments.summary: Overview of the Big Five: Ordovician-Silurian (about 440 million years ago), Late Devonian, Permian-Triassic (the Great Dying), Triassic-Jurassic, and Cretaceous-Paleogene. Mass extinctions are defined loosely, by scale and worldwide reach, and more than twenty events are estimated in Earth's history.

segments.title: Sixth mass extinction and the Anthropocene
segments.summary: The hosts say humans may have made the Big Five into a Big Six, and geologists propose the Anthropocene epoch. They note the risk that a human-driven extinction offers no recovery period, unlike past events.

segments.title: Overkill versus climate change debate
segments.summary: A role-play trip back in time to Australia introduces the overkill hypothesis, in which humans hunted megafauna after arriving about 50,000 years ago. The alternative holds climate change as the main cause. A global study found 177 large mammal species disappeared between 132,000 and 1,000 years ago. Ocean acidification and jellyfish booms are described as current effects.

segments.title: Rediscovered extinct animals
segments.summary: The hosts list animals once thought extinct that reappeared: the Bermuda petrel, the Cuban solenodon, and Gilbert's potoroo, which was thought gone after 1879. They say rediscoveries are not the same as re-engineering.

segments.title: Listener mail: police interrogation follow-up
segments.summary: Listener Matt Pope describes being a nervous witness in a police interview room and playing a defendant in a mock trial, and relates this to the Stanford prison experiment. The hosts respond briefly.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts remind listeners of their social media, email, and website, and point to HowStuffWorks for more on extinction.
